analysis.one_liner: Strips states of their power to block or condition federally permitted water-discharging projects.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: Sen. Barrasso introduced it with four Republican cosponsors, the Environment and Public Works Committee held one hearing, and the Senate never voted before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act, a state can certify, condition, or deny a federal permit for a pipeline, dam, or other project that discharges into waterways. This bill would rewrite that section so states could only examine the applicant's own direct discharge, measured against a narrow list of federal provisions, and would have to act within tight deadlines. The practical effect would be to make it much harder for states to stop or restrict federally permitted energy and industrial projects on water-quality grounds.
analysis.who_benefits: Developers of federally permitted projects that discharge into navigable waters — oil and gas pipelines, hydropower dams, mining and industrial facilities — gain the most, because the states they currently must win over would lose most of their leverage to deny or attach conditions to a certification.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pipeline, dam, and industrial project developers

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the scope of state review so a state may only evaluate 'a discharge made into the navigable waters by the applicant' that results from the federally licensed or permitted activity, rather than broader project effects [S3].

Requires that the decision to grant or deny certification be based only on the applicable provisions of Clean Water Act sections 301, 302, 303, 306, and 307, and that grounds be set forth in writing to the applicant [S3].
Sets a 90-day clock for the certifying state to identify in writing all additional materials needed for a final decision, pressuring states to move quickly and limiting extended reviews [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments lose their primary tool under the Clean Water Act to protect their own waters from federally permitted projects, and residents of those states lose a level of protection they currently rely on when a pipeline, dam, or industrial facility is proposed near their waterways.
analysis.who_pays_short: States and residents relying on state water reviews

drawbacks.text: Narrowing review to the applicant's own discharge would exclude broader project impacts — such as construction activity, erosion, and indirect discharges along a pipeline route — leaving states unable to address them [S3].

The 90-day information-request deadline and written-grounds requirement could force rushed state decisions on complex projects, and federal agencies would effectively become the sole backstop for water quality when a state objects [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For project developers, the bill removes a major regulatory obstacle and would speed permitting. For ordinary people, the cost is the loss of a state-level check that currently lets their own government say no or set conditions when a federally permitted project threatens their waters. Because federal review alone would remain, protections would depend entirely on Washington rather than on the state whose waters are at stake.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held one hearing in August 2018, but the committee never advanced it and the Senate never voted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barrasso introduced the bill on July 31, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
Four Republican senators — Capito, Daines, and Inhofe along with Barrasso — sponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on [S3].
The committee held hearings on the bill, printed as S.Hrg. 115-344, on August 16, 2018 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States and the communities that rely on state water-quality reviews are better off, since the bill died without a vote and state authority under Section 401 was left intact.

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming; bill sponsor and chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee, which held a hearing on it.

for.name: Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, Steve Daines, and James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never reached a floor vote [S3, S4].

industries.note: Pipelines need federal permits under the Clean Water Act, and Section 401 state certifications have been the main tool states use to block or condition pipeline routes; the bill narrows that tool so these projects would face far less state scrutiny. The industry's gain is the public's loss of state water protection.

Relicensing and permitting of dams is a common use of Section 401 certifications; limiting state review to the applicant's direct discharge would ease relicensing and expansion. Cheaper permitting comes at the cost of state-set conditions on downstream water quality.

industries.industry: Mining and industrial facilities needing federal water permits
industries.note: The same 90-day clock and narrowed review standard apply, reducing the ability of states to impose protections on discharges from these facilities.
States would lose most of their authority under Section 401 to protect their own waters, leaving their residents without the state-level review they currently have.
